To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
fidelity was relatively low for the three intervention components and that fidelity to pivotal response training was associated with gains in IQ.

(1) fidelity to pivotal response training was associated with gains in cognition despite relatively low levels of fidelity; (2) fidelity to the other two components of the intervention was not associated with gains in either cognitive ability or adaptive behavior; (3) the STAR program was associated with significant gains in cognition and adaptive behavior, but these gains were not associated with fidelity to any of the three components of the program.

The Strategies for Teaching Based on Autism Research ( STAR ) program is an effective treatment package for young children with autism, but the program was not fully implemented in this study, suggesting the need for new implementation strategies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of interventions for children with autism spectrum disorder.
the active ingredients in interventions for children with autism.
the identification and validation of effective interventions for children with ASD and the dissemination of those interventions to the community.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
fidelity to pivotal response training was associated with gains in IQ and that this association was not mediated by fidelity to the other two components.
fidelity to pivotal response training may be an effective strategy for improving cognitive functioning for students with autism.
the STAR intervention was not effective for the children in this study.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

fidelity to pivotal response training was associated with gains in cognition, and this association was not mediated by fidelity to the other components, but that overall fidelity to all three components was relatively low.
the more fidelity to STAR, the greater the gains for children.
the more we know about what is working, the better we can implement it.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the STAR program, and perhaps other comprehensive treatment packages for children with autism, are not easily implemented in schools and may need to be adapted to meet the needs of students and teachers in under-resourced school settings.
it is possible to identify which components of an evidence-based intervention are most important for achieving desired outcomes, even when fidelity to the entire program is low.

fidelity to each of these components is important, and that the STAR program is a promising intervention package that may have the most impact in settings that have the most resources available to support its implementation.
